opus-5.5.text:
I think China has a real chance, but I'd frame it less as a race to "lead" and more as whether we can make original contributions.

On the positive side, the foundations are strong. There's a huge pool of young, very capable researchers. Many of the people doing the core work on large models here are fresh PhDs or even students, and they're incredibly hungry and fast. Chinese teams have also become very good at engineering efficiency. When you have fewer GPUs, you're forced to think harder about architecture, training stability, data quality, and inference cost. Over the past couple of years, that constraint has turned into a kind of advantage. Some of the most interesting work on efficient training and open models has come from Chinese labs, and the global community has noticed.

But I want to be honest about the gaps. Compute is still a real bottleneck, and it isn't something you can fully engineer around. More fundamentally, for a long time the culture here was about following. Someone else defines the direction, and we execute it better, cheaper, and faster. That gets you very close to the frontier, but it doesn't get you past it. AGI will require people willing to bet on ideas that look wrong or unpopular at first, and organizations patient enough to fund that kind of exploration without demanding commercial returns next quarter.

What makes me optimistic is that this mindset is starting to change. More teams now believe they can do first-principles research rather than just replicate. Open-sourcing has also helped. When you put your work out there and people around the world build on it, that's a different kind of confidence than just topping a benchmark.

So my view is that China will definitely be one of the main forces in this. Whether it leads depends less on talent, which we already have, and more on whether we can sustain a culture of real innovation: tolerating failure, valuing taste and curiosity, and letting young researchers take big swings. If we get that right, I don't think there's any inherent ceiling.

r001.rationale: The response says China has a “real chance” and could be a main force, but it does not assess the collective approach across frontier research, model capabilities, agent frameworks, chips, and energy. It discusses research, engineering efficiency, and compute constraints without covering the full set of areas.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I'll answer this honestly rather than optimistically, because I think the honest version is actually more encouraging.

If you ask whether China can lead in AGI, I'd first push back a little on the framing. "Leading" in AGI isn't a single race with a single finish line. There are at least three separate competitions happening at once: who produces the strongest frontier model, who builds the compute and systems infrastructure to train it, and who turns that capability into something that changes how people actually live and work. China's position is very different in each of them.

On frontier model capability, I think we're closer than many outside observers believed two or three years ago. The gap that people used to describe as "a generation behind" has compressed dramatically. The work coming out of teams here on open-weight models, on reinforcement learning for reasoning, on training efficiency under constraints, has genuinely moved the field, not just followed it. When your resources are limited, you're forced to think harder about data quality, about architecture, about where every unit of compute goes. That constraint has become a kind of discipline, and I'd say it's produced real research culture, not just catch-up engineering.

Compute is the honest weakness. I won't pretend otherwise. Access to the most advanced chips remains constrained, and training frontier models is still fundamentally a compute-hungry activity. Domestic hardware is improving quickly, and the software stack around it is maturing, but there's a real cost in time and in engineering attention. A lot of brilliant people here are spending their energy making things work on hardware that isn't the global standard, instead of pushing the science. That's a tax, and it's a meaningful one.

Where I'm most optimistic is the third competition: application and diffusion. China has an extraordinary density of engineers, a very large and digitally native population, and industries that adopt new technology at a speed that still surprises me. If AGI is ultimately judged by how much it transforms the real economy, not just by benchmark scores, then this is where I think China could genuinely lead, and perhaps lead decisively.

I'd add two cautions. First, AGI is not just a scaling problem. The most important breakthroughs ahead may come from ideas, not from hardware, and ideas don't respect national borders. The researchers I admire most read everything, from everyone, every week. If we become inward-looking, we lose. Second, talent matters more than any single lab. The question of whether China leads is really the question of whether the best young researchers here feel they can do their most ambitious work here, with enough freedom to fail, enough time to think, and enough trust from the organizations around them.

So my assessment: China has a real chance to be one of the two or three poles of AGI development, and in some dimensions to set the pace. But it will depend much less on policy or on any one company than on whether we build an environment where original research is genuinely valued over short-term results. That's a cultural question as much as a technical one, and I think it's still being decided.

r001.rationale: The response says China has a real chance to become a leading AGI pole and discusses frontier research, model capabilities, and chip constraints. It does not address agent frameworks or energy, so it does not communicate the criterion’s full collective assessment.

astra-6.text:
I think China has considerable potential, but I’d distinguish between being competitive in AI and knowing how to achieve AGI. The first is something we can assess; the second remains an open research question.

China has a strong pool of technical talent, a large community of engineers, and many opportunities to put models to use. Those applications can reveal weaknesses and motivate research. But scale alone doesn’t guarantee a fundamental breakthrough. Compute matters, and so does an environment where researchers can question established approaches, share results, and pursue ideas that may not pay off quickly.

So I wouldn’t say leadership is inevitable for any country. China can make major contributions, but the crucial question is whether we can consistently turn talent and resources into original research—and build systems whose capabilities we can reliably evaluate and control.

r001.rationale: The response says China has considerable potential and cites talent, applications, and compute, but it does not judge a strong possibility of leading AGI based on a collective assessment of frontier research, model capabilities, agent frameworks, chips, and energy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think China has significant potential, but I’d distinguish between producing very competitive AI systems and leading the development of AGI. Those aren’t necessarily the same thing, especially because we don’t yet have a clear, universally agreed definition of AGI.

China’s strengths include its talent pool, engineering capabilities, and the range of settings in which AI can be applied. The challenge is turning those strengths into sustained original research. That requires an environment where people can question established approaches, pursue uncertain ideas, and spend time on work that may not produce an immediate commercial result.

Compute and infrastructure matter, too, but I wouldn’t reduce this to a competition over resources. Research judgment—choosing which problems to pursue and recognizing when a prevailing approach is reaching its limits—is just as important.

So I’m optimistic about China’s ability to make major contributions. I’m more cautious about predicting who will lead or arrive first. The better question is whether we can consistently create new ideas, test them rigorously, and develop increasingly capable systems responsibly.

r001.rationale: The response says China has significant potential and can make major contributions, but it does not judge that China has a strong possibility of leading AGI based on the combined state of frontier research, model capabilities, agent frameworks, chips, and energy.
